title: Wasps Are Vanishing This Summer, and Scientists Are Alarmed
summary:
Summer 2026 in the UK is unusually quiet — not because of a lack of picnics, but because of a lack of wasps. Normally, warm weather brings out more wasps, and last year headlines warned of "plagues of wasps." This year, even pest controllers report very few calls to remove nests. As a wasp biologist, I've noticed it acutely: my students need wasps for experiments, and we simply can't find them.

Wasps are not just picnic pests. They are important ecosystem players: they control pests, pollinate flowers, and decompose dead matter. Their absence is worrying. So what's going on? Spring 2026 began warm and dry, which should have been good for wasps. New queens, called foundresses, emerged from hibernation to start nests alone. But then came unprecedented heat for the time of year, followed by cold, damp days and chilly nights. These extremes may have caused queens to abandon their nests or die.

Then came the heatwaves. Insects have a thermal tolerance called critical thermal maximum (CTmax). If exceeded, they suffer desiccation, muscle spasms, and stupor. For wasps, CTmax is around 45°C (113°F). This summer, ground surfaces in the UK exceeded 50°C. That's lethal. Even sublethal heat can impair behavior and productivity. For example, bumblebee cognition is impaired by heatwaves of 32°C. Wasps are thought to be resilient, but their CTmax may be lower than other social insects, making them vulnerable.

The few wasps seen this summer are also unusually small. Adult size is fixed during larval development, depending on food quality and quantity. Heat can cause larvae to develop faster and pupate at a smaller size. Global warming is thought to explain a trend of shrinking social wasps over the last 100 years. We may be seeing this in real-time.

The Big Wasp Survey, the only national monitoring effort, will start sampling later this summer. If data confirm the decline, it could signal a serious ecological problem. So next time a wasp approaches your meal, don't flap it away. Watch what it wants. It might be desperate for protein or sugar — just trying to survive.
why_it_matters: Insects pollinate crops, recycle nutrients, and keep pest species in check, so a summer with almost no wasps is a warning about how quickly extreme weather can disrupt food webs that humans depend on.

questions.question: Why is this summer described as unusually quiet in the UK?
options: The weather has been colder than in a typical summer.
Far fewer wasps than normal are being seen.
There have been fewer picnics than usual.
Schools closed early for the holidays.
questions.correct_answer: Far fewer wasps than normal are being seen.

questions.question: According to the article, what three roles do wasps play in ecosystems?
options: They control pests, pollinate flowers, and decompose dead matter.
They pollinate flowers, build honey, and feed birds.
They decompose wood, make silk, and feed livestock.
They control pests, spread seeds, and clean rivers.
questions.correct_answer: They control pests, pollinate flowers, and decompose dead matter.

questions.question: What is the wasps' critical thermal maximum, and what happened this summer?
options: About 50°C, and ground surfaces stayed below it.
About 32°C, and air temperatures reached 40°C.
About 113°C, and nothing close to it occurred.
About 45°C, and ground surfaces in the UK exceeded 50°C.
questions.correct_answer: About 45°C, and ground surfaces in the UK exceeded 50°C.

questions.question: Why are this summer's wasps unusually small?
options: Heat can make larvae develop faster and pupate at a smaller size.
They have been eating only sugar instead of protein.
They are simply younger than the wasps of previous years.
They belong to a different species than usual.
questions.correct_answer: Heat can make larvae develop faster and pupate at a smaller size.

questions.question: How did spring weather affect the new queens?
options: Constant rain helped them build nests faster.
Unprecedented heat for the time of year, followed by cold damp days and chilly nights, may have made them abandon nests or die.
Snow and frost killed every foundress in the country.
Warm, dry weather had no effect on them at all.
questions.correct_answer: Unprecedented heat for the time of year, followed by cold damp days and chilly nights, may have made them abandon nests or die.

questions.question: What role does the Big Wasp Survey play?
options: It measures how many picnics happen each summer.
It breeds new wasp colonies in laboratories.
It removes wasp nests from people's homes.
It starts sampling later this summer and is the only national monitoring effort.
questions.correct_answer: It starts sampling later this summer and is the only national monitoring effort.

background_read: Wasps belong to the same insect order as bees and ants (Hymenoptera), but they get a fraction of the public sympathy and research funding that bees receive, which is one reason monitoring efforts are so limited.

In a typical colony, only newly produced queens survive the winter; they hibernate alone and must build a nest from scratch in spring, chewing wood into a paper-like pulp — a fragile moment when bad weather can wipe out a whole year's offspring.
Because insects are cold-blooded, their body temperature follows their surroundings, so extreme heat is directly dangerous rather than just uncomfortable.

Scientists have documented falling insect numbers and biomass in several countries; a long-running study in Germany, for example, found that the total mass of flying insects caught in traps had dropped sharply over a few decades, though wasps were rarely measured directly.

Europe has seen record-breaking summer heat in recent years, and the UK has only recently started recording days above 40°C — a threshold that would matter hugely for insects whose CTmax sits near 45°C.

perspectives.description: Researchers see the quiet summer as a possible ecological alarm bell, especially since wasps are understudied compared with bees. If the Big Wasp Survey confirms a decline, it would suggest heatwaves are harming even insects assumed to be tough and resilient.

Wasps naturally rise and fall in numbers from year to year, and reports from pest controllers are anecdotal rather than measured. Some scientists would argue that without long-term data, it is too early to call this a collapse rather than a bad season.

Many people dislike wasps and may even welcome fewer of them, seeing only the stings and the swarming around food. The article challenges that view by pointing out the pest control, pollination, and decomposition services wasps provide free of charge.

The bigger question is whether governments will fund long-term insect monitoring instead of relying on one volunteer survey, and whether heat-adaptation measures such as shade and water in gardens can help insects survive hotter summers. Small choices next summer could determine what the data show.
